cards.canonical_statement: For every coordinate dimension n, measurable region s containing distinct points x,y, and vector c, there exists an everywhere Fréchet-differentiable map constantly equal to c which is not injective on s. Differentiability alone therefore does not establish the injectivity hypothesis of a coordinate change.
cards.proof_strategy: Choose the constant map with arbitrary value c.
sketch_steps: Choose the constant map with arbitrary value c.
Its Fréchet derivative exists everywhere and is the zero continuous linear map.
The two distinct domain points x and y have the same image c.
Thus the map fails injectivity on the region despite differentiability; the substitution theorem needs its separate injectivity premise.

cards.canonical_statement: For arbitrary n, let f be injective on a measurable region s with within-s derivative D, and let g be injective on f(s) with within-f(s) derivative E. For every real F integrable on g(f(s)), the twice-pulled-back density |det D(x)| (|det E(f(x))| F(g(f(x)))) is integrable on s, and its integral equals the integral of F on g(f(s)). The second derivative is evaluated at the intermediate point f(x).
cards.proof_strategy: The first injective differentiable substitution takes the measurable region s to a measurable intermediate image f(s).
sketch_steps: The first injective differentiable substitution takes the measurable region s to a measurable intermediate image f(s).
Apply integrability transport to g on this intermediate domain, obtaining the inner weighted density.
Transport its integrability through f to establish integrability of the twice-weighted density on s.
Apply the Jacobian integral formula first to g and then to f.
The second substitution evaluates both the intermediate density and E at f(x), and multiplies the two absolute determinant factors.
Combine the equalities while retaining both region-specific injectivity and within-derivative assumptions.
